Little understood fact about vocal interfaces (Google Assistant, Siri, Cortana, Echo, etc.) is that (in certain respects), they are just like a search engine but with only one result.

Whenever you ask them a general knowledge question (one not pertaining to you own data such as calendar, e-mail, etc.), they will either fetch a predetermined response (only one at a time, notwithstanding caching/batching/prediction) from a database or, when the answer is not in the database, they will launch a query to their respective affiliated search engine (Google, Bing, etc.) and only give you the 1st result. Unless you ask for more, in which case they will give you the 2nd, 3rd result, etc. (one at time).

.

Imagine doing a Duck Duck Go/Google/Bing search and only getting one result. Then click next if the 1st result doesn't satisfy you. You would be more susceptible to manipulative 1st results that are part of the desired (correct) narrative.

.

This is a property of all vocal interfaces, not just theirs.

The eyes can be presented with multiple blobs of information at the same time, and each person will do their thing: Some will read all titles and do their own ranking in their head, others will succinctly scan the results and click on what catches their eye. I find myself using both depending on the context.

You can't do that with voice. Each blob of information needs to be presented sequentially, and the listener needs to wait an incompressible amount of time to hear and digest 10 results, thus being more inclined to forego the 2nd and subsequent results.
